capacity_loss_basis.derivation: MODELED assumption - not a sourced figure and never to be presented as one. No sourced capacity-loss fraction exists for LA 2021: the source record quantifies queues and waits, not capacity loss, and berth throughput did not collapse (the Port of Los Angeles was on track for a record ~10.7M TEU in 2021, Port of Los Angeles release, 20 Dec 2021), so no throughput-drop derivation is defensible. Model: at the 10 Nov 2021 MESocal snapshot the complex held 109 container ships waiting and 30 at berth; capacity_loss is set to the waiting share of container ships present, 109 / (109 + 30) = 0.78 (rounded to 2 dp) - a stock-share proxy for the share of container-ship flow the berth/landside system was not serving at the peak snapshot, NOT a measured throughput drop. The binding constraint was landside (dwell/driver channel), not berth capacity. Any scorecard printing LA results must print this modeled assumption alongside them. (An earlier version carried capacity_loss as null; the engine then silently substituted its 0.5 default for congestion-kind specs.)
capacity_loss_basis.source: Marine Exchange of Southern California (MESocal) 10 Nov 2021 report, via Western Overseas: https://www.westernoverseas.com/port-congestion-update-11-12-21/ (same report already cited for the 2021-11-10 observed steps in this dataset)

disruption_notes: capacity_loss 0.78 is a MODELED value (see capacity_loss_basis in the disruption spec for the full derivation): the source timeline quantifies queue counts and waits, not a capacity-loss fraction, and no sourced figure is claimed. The binding constraint was landside (dwell/driver channel), not berth capacity. expected_duration_d 58 = 2021-09-19 (first dated record in the timeline) to 2021-11-16 (offshore queuing system takes effect) - the window covered by the source timeline, not the full historical episode. Pre-pandemic baseline: the complex had never seen a backlog greater than 17 ships (MESocal).
